newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil urged to forge ahead with telecom opening.
newsitem.headline: Brazil urged to forge ahead with telecom opening.

text.p: Brazil should forge ahead with the privatization of its telecommunications sector, open its local wire-line loop to competition and end limits to foreign ownership in the sector, a U.S. Congressman said.
"There is no justification at all for a foreign ownership limitation," Rep. Jack Fields, R-Texas, told a group of stock market analysts.
The United States now imposes a 25-percent cap on foreign ownership of U.S. telecom operators, but that will probably be scrapped by Congress in the coming months, he said.
Brazil has put a 49 percent limit on foreign capital ownership of telecom companies scheduled to be privatized.

Fields, chairman of the U.S. House of Representative's Telecommunication and Finance Subcommittee, is in Brazil at the invitation of the Brazilian Congress's telecommunications committee and lobbying on behalf of U.S. telecoms firms.
Brazil is now in the process of drafting legislation and creating a regulatory body to oversee its promising telecoms sector, which is to be privatized in the coming years.
Speaking at the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, Fields said Brazil and China are viewed by U.S. telecoms firms as the most attractive markets in the world due to their vast size and potential for growth.

"Brazil and China are the No. 1 interest of our telecoms companies," he said. "There's no scientific poll, no white paper that says that, but that's what I hear from talking with CEOs and chairmen of major companies."
Brazil may have an edge because it is farther ahead in the privatization process, expected to begin in 1998, he said.

"The plus here (in Brazil) is that the privatization process has begun and it's recognized. There's going to be an explosion here and a very positive explosion in terms of jobs and consumer empowerment," Fields said.

U.S. firms, he added, are particularly interested in the B Band cellular concessions, slated to begin late this year or early in 1997, and positioning themselves for the selloff of Brazil's federally owned Telebras.
Fields said the break up of American Telephone & Telegraph Co. (AT&T) is a model that can be applied to the Telebras system, made up of 27 local operators and a long-distance monopoly.
Today, AT&T has a smaller percentage share of the U.S. market but revenues are up while consumers have benefitted from lower prices and a greater array of services, he said.

He declined to name U.S. firms interested in Brazil market but said some are already here and eyeing all aspects of the local market. "This market is like China's. It's too big not to be here." he said.
Fields espoused the virtues of the free market and urged Brazil to open the "local loop."
"The loop I refer to is the actually all of the equipment, all of the wiring of the telephone companies," he said. "If that's not open, then I don't see the predicate for a truly open system."

Emerging markets, like Brazil, have the advantage of learning from legislative and regulatory mistakes made in the U.S. over the last 20 years, especially in cable and cellular services, he added. "You can jump over all these obstacles and all the old technology we're now having to depreciate," he said.
